newsitem.title: USA: New England Electric in $1.675 billion deal with PG&E.
newsitem.headline: New England Electric in $1.675 billion deal with PG&E.

text.p: In a move that could hasten deregulation of New England's electric power industry, New England Electric System said Wednesday it agreed to sell its non-nuclear generating business to an affiliate of PG&E Corp. for $1.59 billion in cash.
The result will be cheaper electricity for customers but at least 1,600 layoffs, executives said.
The deal with U.S. Generating Co., an affiliate of PG&E, was the first in the nation in which a utility has sold its generating assets. It will require both federal and state regulatory approval.

The acquisition, for $1.59 billion in cash plus $85 million to cover severance costs, puts pressure on the Massachusetts Legislature to approve quickly an option that allows ratepayers to chose their electricity suppliers.

The Westborough, Mass.-based company's 1.3 million ratepayers will see the price of electricity drop between 15 and 18 percent following the sale of the 18 power plants and 23 power contract obligations of more than 5,000 megawatts, NEES Chief Executive Officer John Rowe said.
NEES is a $2.3 billion public utility holding company. Its retail and wholesale power units, New England Power Co. and Narragansett Electric Co., supply customers in Massachusetts and Rhode Island.

Asked how many of the company's 4,800 workers would lose their jobs, Rowe said, "We believe that when this transaction is consumated, we will need something on the order of 3,200 workers in the retail business," he said. NEES currently employs 4,800 workers. "That's a 1,600 employee difference."
U.S. Generating Chief Executive P. Crisman Iribe said, "These facilities are heading into a competitive environment and cost and cost control is extremely important."

New England is at the frontier of electricity deregulation, where once-highly regulated utilities are now being told they have to compete for customers. Rhode Island will be fully deregulated beginning Jan. 1, 1998, and New Hamsphire will not be far behind.
But Massachusetts has not formally approved its regulatory agency's plan to allow consumers a choice of electric supplier or, if they choose not to select a supplier, receive a 10 percent rate cut.

The $1.59 billion includes $225 million to be paid when customer choice of power supplier becomes avaiable to either 50 percent of New England or 89 percent of Massachusetts. That amount begins to decline if choice is not available by Jan.1, 1999. If the Massachusetts Legislature fails to approve the option, neither goal will be reached.

U.S. Generating paid about $600 million more than the book value of NEES's assets, Rowe said. It will retire nearly all of NEES's fossil, hydro and nuclear power stranded costs as powerplants that can no longer be operated profitably. NEES still will have about $900 million of stranded costs stemming from nuclear plant decommissioning and regulatory assets.
In anticipation of the sale, the NEES board authorised the repurchase of up to five million of its common shares.
For U.S. Generating, the deal will expand its presence in New England and more than double its present 3,375 megawatt capacity nationwide.
New England Electric's stock was up $1.75 to $38.75 and PG&E was down 18.75 cents at $24.125, both on the New York Stock Exchange in afternoon trading.
